bread_ration.name: bread ration
bread_ration.lore: Roman legionaries marched on bucellatum, bread baked twice until it could survive a campaign and break a tooth. This loaf keeps the tradition. Soaked in water it becomes edible; dry, it becomes a test of character. It fills the belly and keeps a delver walking, which is all anyone asks of it.

dried_meat.name: dried meat
dried_meat.lore: Salt and smoke have kept meat through winters and sieges since before anyone wrote the method down. These strips are wound tight in waxed cloth and come from no animal the wrapper admits to. They chew like bootlaces and sustain like a proper meal.

hard_cheese.name: hard cheese
hard_cheese.lore: Odysseus and his men found the Cyclops's cave stacked with racks of cheese and helped themselves before the owner came home. A cave-aged wheel like this one would have been worth the risk. The rind is thick as bark and the heart is dense, salty, and good for a long march.

wild_mushroom.name: wild mushroom
wild_mushroom.lore: A pale cap from the dungeon's damp corners, faintly luminous at the gills. Foragers above ground say there are old mushroom hunters and bold mushroom hunters, but no old, bold ones. Down here the glowing kind is safe: filling, earthy, and mildly restorative to small hurts.

apple.name: apple
apple.lore: Genesis never names the fruit in Eden. The apple took the blame later, helped by a Latin pun: malum means both 'apple' and 'evil'. This one is innocent, crisp and cold, and impossibly fresh for its depth. It quiets hunger and leaves small hurts feeling a little mended.

trail_rations.name: trail rations
trail_rations.lore: A waxed parcel of dried fruit, salted crackers, hard tack, and a sealed jar of rendered fat. Nobody has ever praised the flavor. Experienced delvers pack it anyway, because it is the most filling thing that fits in a satchel and it never spoils.

healing_herb.name: healing herb
healing_herb.lore: Yarrow carries the name Achillea because Achilles is said to have packed his soldiers' wounds with it at Troy, having learned the art from the centaur Chiron. Monks grew it in their physic gardens for the same purpose. Chewed, the bitter leaves do little for hunger and a good deal for bleeding.

elvish_bread.name: elvish bread
elvish_bread.lore: Old tales warn travelers never to eat at the Fair Folk's table, since one bite can keep a guest under the hill for a hundred years. This pale loaf seems to be the exception, baked for the road and not for the snare. It is light as a wafer, faintly sweet, and one piece carries a traveler farther than a full pack of rations.

hearty_stew.name: hearty stew
hearty_stew.lore: Esau came in from the field famished and sold his birthright to his brother Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew. A sealed clay pot of this, still warm, explains the temptation. It is thick with roots and tender meat, and it puts back both strength and blood.

deep_fungi.name: deep fungi
deep_fungi.lore: These mushrooms grow only in the lowest passages, where no light has ever fallen, feeding on whatever seeps from enchanted stone. The first bite sets the head spinning. Then the body steadies, well fed, and comes away subtly changed: a little stronger, or quicker, or sharper than before.

void_ration.name: void ration
void_ration.lore: A dark brick of pressed provisions from the abyssal floors, where ordinary food rots in an hour. Nobody knows who presses them. Eating one fills the limbs with a cold, steady vigor that lingers as real fighting strength, and hunger becomes a rumor for a long while after.

philosopher_tea.name: philosopher's tea
philosopher_tea.lore: Chinese legend says the emperor Shennong was boiling water under a wild tree when a few leaves drifted into the pot, and he liked what happened. Sages have steeped leaves ever since. This violet tea, gathered near old ruins, settles the mind and leaves it lastingly wiser. Scholars claim hard questions seem to wait politely for an answer.

ambrosia.name: Ambrosia
ambrosia.lore: The food of the Olympian gods. Homer uses the word loosely: it is eaten, it is drunk, and Thetis anoints the dead Patroclus with it to keep his body from decay. Doves carried it to Zeus. It was never meant for mortal tongues. A mortal who tastes it is fed, healed, and bettered in every part.

golden_apple.name: Golden Apple of Hesperides
golden_apple.lore: Gaia gave Hera a tree of golden apples as a wedding gift, and Hera set it at the western edge of the world with the Hesperides to tend it and the serpent Ladon coiled around the trunk. For his eleventh labor Heracles held up the sky while Atlas fetched three. One bite fills, heals, and toughens the body for good.

peach_of_immortality.name: Peach of Immortality
peach_of_immortality.lore: Xi Wangmu, Queen Mother of the West, grows these peaches in her heavenly orchard, where the slowest trees ripen once in nine thousand years. Journey to the West tells how Sun Wukong, set to guard the orchard, ate the best of them himself. Even one mends the body, fills it, and leaves some lasting gift behind.

tantalus_plum.name: Tantalus's Plum
tantalus_plum.unidentified_name: a perfect-looking fruit just out of reach
tantalus_plum.lore: Tantalus served his own son to the gods to test whether they knew everything. They did. In the underworld he stands in a pool that drains when he stoops to drink, under boughs that lift their fruit when he reaches. This is one of that fruit. It heals deep wounds and, true to its tree, barely touches hunger.

magic_dungeon_carrot.name: Magic Dungeon Carrot
magic_dungeon_carrot.lore: A carrot that glows faintly orange and smells of wildflowers, grown in some enchanted bed far from any sun. It is perfectly good to eat. Rumor holds that a certain magical beast deeper in the dungeon loves nothing better, and that a wise traveler keeps one in the pack for that meeting.
